## THE CURRENT MAP
12:36/q01 How does the verse indicate Joseph's imprisonment? [وَدَخَلَ ٱلسِّجْنَ · rhetoric]
  12:36/q01/p1 It leaves his imprisonment unstated and implies it through the youths' entry with him. — reasons: Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi identify the omitted prior event, 'they imprisoned him'; Ibn al-Jawzi relays al-Zajjaj.
  12:36/q01/p2 The wording itself shows Joseph was already imprisoned. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj says entry into prison with him establishes his imprisonment; al-Wahidi reports the inference.
12:36/q02 What does 'with him' say about when the youths entered? [مَعَهُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether maʿa requires concurrence when the entry began.)
  12:36/q02/p1 They entered prison together with Joseph at the same time. — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take maʿa as newly begun companionship; Abu Hayyan says it denotes a new shared event; al-Biqaʿi cites him. Al-Alusi prefers concurrence as the original sense, while comparing 27:44. Al-Suyūṭī gives shared time or place as a basic sense of maʿa, while analyzing it as a noun.
  12:36/q02/p2 The wording allows different times; it only establishes shared confinement. — reasons: Ibn ʿAtiyya allows simultaneous or separate admission. Al-Qurtubi allows before, after or together and says the verse only requires the same room. Al-Zarkashī says maʿa marks shared participation in an action or ruling without necessarily requiring simultaneity; al-Suyūṭī cites association apart from shared time or place.
12:36/q03 Why place 'with him' before 'prison,' and what might the wording imply? [مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ · rhetoric] (turns on: The force of maʿa and the emphasis conveyed by word order.)
  12:36/q03/p1 The order emphasizes companionship, with Joseph as the focus. — reasons: Al-Alusi says the object precedes the subject for emphasis and companionship precedes prison because it matters more; he cites 18:62. He distinguishes ongoing Islam from punctual entry and invokes 27:44. Al-Suyūṭī reports al-Rāghib's point that the complement of maʿa receives the intended focus.
  12:36/q03/p2 Their entry with him may have made imprisonment easier through his presence. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this possibility.
  12:36/q03/p3 The expression associates Joseph with their prison state while leaving his choice of it unstated. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this explanation and observes that maʿa normally implies concurrence from the action's beginning.
  12:36/q03/p4 'With' can express joining another in obedience rather than exact simultaneous action. — reasons: Al-Kashf's comparison is the Queen's 'I submitted with Solomon' (27:44): she enters submission to God and the Messenger following prophetic guidance, despite earlier religious self-understanding.
12:36/q04 How is 'prison' pronounced and understood here? [ٱلسِّجْنَ · readings] (turns on: The vocalization and whether the noun denotes place or act.)
  12:36/q04/p1 With kasra, it means the place of confinement. — reasons: Ibn ʿAshur says all readers use kasra because one enters a place, not the act of imprisoning. Ibn al-Jazarī says all readers agree on kasra at 12:36 and related prison mentions; the fatḥa of Yaʿqūb belongs to 12:33 and marks the verbal noun.
  12:36/q04/p2 With fatḥa, al-sajn denotes the prison location. — reasons: Al-Alusi gives this vocalization in explaining the clause after implied 'they imprisoned him.'
12:36/q05 Why are the prisoners called 'two youths'? [فَتَيَانِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the designation concerns age, service status or their mutual conduct.)
  12:36/q05/p1 Fatā can designate an enslaved man or servant regardless of age. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj allows young or old slaves; al-Mawardi says slaves are so called; al-Qushayri also permits free servants; Ibn ʿAtiyya allows literal youth, slave, or free servant. Ibn al-Anbari ties it to being owned. Al-Tabataba'i takes them as young male slaves.
  12:36/q05/p2 They are called youths because neither tried to outdo the other's claim and each deferred to his companion. — reasons: Al-Tustari gives this ethical explanation.
  12:36/q05/p3 They are literally young men accompanying Joseph into prison. — reasons: Al-Dāmaghānī glosses the two fityān as the young men who entered alongside Joseph.
12:36/q06 What is the form of 'two youths'? [فَتَيَانِ · grammar]
  12:36/q06/p1 It is the dual of fatā, a weak-y noun. — reasons: Al-Nahhas identifies the dual; al-Qurtubi notes the irregular form al-futu. Sībawayh explains that the dual of fatā reveals its original yāʾ, hence fatayān; the wāw of futuwwa follows the preceding ḍamma rather than proving a wāw root. Related forms and imāla can expose the underlying consonant.
12:36/q07 Who were the two prisoners and whom did they serve? [فَتَيَانِ · referent] (turns on: Whether external reports are used to fill the Quran's unnamed roles.)
  12:36/q07/p1 They were the Egyptian king's baker or food steward and cupbearer or wine steward. — reasons: Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and many commentators assign food and drink duties; the wine vision belongs to the cupbearer and bread vision to the baker. Ibn ʿAshur says the Quran leaves offences unspecified; Asad cites the Bible for the offices; Islahi stresses that the Quran does not identify them. Al-Razi says Joseph could infer royal service from their later use of rabb for their master in 12:41-42. Al-Dāmaghānī explicitly identifies the wine dreamer as the king's cupbearer.
  12:36/q07/p2 The Quran leaves their identities unnamed. — reasons: Islahi states this limitation explicitly; Asad says the Bible identifies the offices without conflict with the Quran.
12:36/q08 What names are reported for the king and the two servants? [فَتَيَانِ · reports] (turns on: The transmitted personal names differ beyond spelling variants.)
  12:36/q08/p1 Ibn Ishaq's pair is Majlath or Mujlith and Nabu or Nabwa; the latter serves drink. — reasons: The names vary in spelling: Mujlith/Majlath/Mujlab and Nabu/Nabwa/Banu/Bunū. King-name order varies: al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid or al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan; Baghawi adds ibn Sharwan. Al-Suhayli could not retain the baker's name.
  12:36/q08/p2 The servants were Sharham Aqam and Sharham Asham. — reasons: Muqatil gives these fuller names.
  12:36/q08/p3 The cupbearer was Manja and the baker Majlath. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites Kaʿb via al-Thaʿlabi.
  12:36/q08/p4 They were Sharham and Sarham. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites al-Naqqash. Al-Suyūṭī also transmits the Sharham and Sarham naming.
  12:36/q08/p5 The men were Mijlath and his sons, including the cupbearer. — reasons: Al-Suyūṭī reports this identification.
  12:36/q08/p6 The men were Rāshān and Marṭash. — reasons: Al-Suyūṭī relays this alternative identification.
12:36/q09 Why were the royal servants imprisoned? [وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ فَتَيَانِ · reports] (turns on: Whether the report describes suspicion alone, an actual poisoned meal, or reciprocal accusation.)
  12:36/q09/p1 The baker was suspected of trying to poison the king, and the cupbearer of complicity. — reasons: Al-Suddi reports suspicion, not proven execution; several later accounts repeat it. Asad says the Quran does not specify their offences; Ibn ʿAshur notes royal anger and an unnamed poisoning report.
  12:36/q09/p2 Both were implicated in a planned poisoning, but the cupbearer withdrew while the baker accepted and poisoned food. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabi and Baghawi describe bribery, warning, animal test and the poisoned meal; al-Qurtubi and Bursevi relay the same basic split.
  12:36/q09/p3 Conspirators pushed both to poison food and drink and the two accused one another. — reasons: Kuranyolu gives this report.
12:36/q10 What happened to Joseph on entering prison? [وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجْنَ · reports] (turns on: Different reports emphasize public punishment or Joseph's reception inside prison.)
  12:36/q10/p1 He was paraded in chains on a donkey and chose this hardship over Hell. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi attributes the report to Wahb and others; it frames the punishment as a consequence of refusing his mistress.
  12:36/q10/p2 He encouraged hopeless prisoners, won their affection, and was offered favorable quarters. — reasons: Qatada and later reports describe counsel about patience, reward, purification and hope; the keeper could improve confinement but not free him. Al-Durr also reports a severe reply from Joseph to the keeper about the Fire's mountains.
12:36/q11 What did Joseph say when people in prison loved him? [فَتَيَانِ · reports]
  12:36/q11/p1 He warned the two men or jailer that love for him had previously brought hardship. — reasons: Versions name his aunt's love and theft accusation, his father's love and the well, and the Aziz's wife's love and prison; some omit the aunt. The men nevertheless persisted; al-Mawardi adds that Joseph wanted only his Lord's love.
12:36/q12 How did Joseph identify himself in prison? [* · reports]
  12:36/q12/p1 He named his lineage through Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham. — reasons: Qatada's account, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Durr preserve the lineage; Abu Hayyan adds epithets 'God's chosen,' 'sacrificed one' and 'friend.' The keeper offered what treatment he could.
12:36/q13 How did the two men come to ask Joseph for interpretation? [قَالَ أَحَدُهُمَآ نَبِّئْنَا · reports] (turns on: Whether their approach followed a deliberate test or genuine distress and observed trust.)
  12:36/q13/p1 Joseph had announced or demonstrated that he could interpret dreams, and they tested him. — reasons: Al-Suddi, Ibn Masud and others say the men feigned dreams; al-Tabari says they first asked about his knowledge. Abu Hayyan says he told prisoners his skill, while al-Razi allows prior demonstration. Study Quran reports they had seen him interpret others.
  12:36/q13/p2 They were troubled or curious about unusual dreams and trusted his knowledge and piety. — reasons: Ibn Abbas reports troubled waking; al-Razi says they may have mentioned their sadness; Islah

i says they had observed his knowledge and piety. Ibn ʿAshur says prisoners exchanged dreams for conversation and hoped for signs of release; Egyptian interpretation was familiar.
12:36/q14 Did both prisoners actually have the dreams they recounted? [إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ وَقَالَ ٱلْءَاخَرُ إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ · reports] (turns on: The transmitted accounts conflict; requests for interpretation and arānī are offered as evidence for genuine dreams.)
  12:36/q14/p1 Both truly dreamed. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and Mujahid report actual dreams, and Ibn Abbas describes troubled waking; al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi argue that requesting interpretation implies dreams because waking sight needs none. Al-Razi adds that arānī would otherwise be unnecessary. Ibn Kathir prefers this as the majority view.
  12:36/q14/p2 Neither dreamed; both invented accounts to test Joseph. — reasons: Ibn Masud, al-Suddi and al-Shaʿbi report fabrication; Mujahid also relates their later claim that they were joking, after which Joseph said the matter was settled. Al-Durr gives the subsequent interpretations and request to remember Joseph. Baghawi notes contrary reports.
  12:36/q14/p3 Only the baker, later crucified, lied; the cupbearer dreamed truthfully. — reasons: Abu Mijlaz and an Imam report identify the crucified man as the liar; Bursevi repeats this resolution.
12:36/q15 How does the first man's dream scene unfold? [إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰنِىٓ أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا · reports] (turns on: Reports vary in whether the vine was planted and in details of its branches and clusters.)
  12:36/q15/p1 He pressed grapes from three clusters into the king's cup and served him. — reasons: Muqatil, Mujahid and later transmitters give three clusters, sometimes on a three-branched vine or in a garden; Ibn Abbas also reports the cup for the king. Bursevi describes the service.
  12:36/q15/p2 He planted a vine, pressed its grapes, and served the king. — reasons: Ikrima adds that Joseph foretold release after three days and resumed wine service.
  12:36/q15/p3 The vision matches the cupbearer's ordinary occupation: pressing grapes for wine. — reasons: Al-Razi notes both visions mirror the men's professions; Study Quran connects this vision with the wine carrier and 12:41.
12:36/q16 How does 'I see myself' mark a dream rather than waking action? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · rhetoric]
  12:36/q16/p1 It recounts a past dream scene; the sleep setting is understood. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj says sleep need not be named; Ibn al-Anbari says simple 'I press' would otherwise suffice. Al-Razi cites arānī plus the request for interpretation. Al-Tabataba'i notes the break before 'one of them said' separates the dream scene from prison entry.
12:36/q17 How does the verb 'I see myself' take its objects? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · grammar] (turns on: Whether aṣiru fills a second object slot or states the dreamer's circumstance.)
  12:36/q17/p1 As a cognition verb, it allows subject and object pronouns to refer to the same person. — reasons: Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi contrast ordinary verbs, which need a separate reflexive expression; al-Samin adds that causative hamza yields a third object, citing 8:43.
  12:36/q17/p2 'I press' is the second object of the dream cognition verb. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this parsing.
  12:36/q17/p3 'I press' is a circumstantial clause. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this alternative.
12:36/q18 How is the yāʾ of the two 'I see myself' forms read? [أَرَىٰنِىٓ · readings] (turns on: Length of the final yāʾ in recitation.)
  12:36/q18/p1 The standard form has a short final yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records the standard at both occurrences.
  12:36/q18/p2 A canonical variant extends the final yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records the extension at both occurrences. Ibn al-Jazarī lists the two dream phrases among Yūsuf's open yāʾs and names the Medinan readers, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr in the relevant lists.
12:36/q19 How is the yāʾ of the two 'indeed I' forms read? [إِنِّىٓ · readings] (turns on: Length of the final yāʾ in recitation.)
  12:36/q19/p1 The standard form ends in a short yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records this at both occurrences.
  12:36/q19/p2 A canonical recitational variant extends the yāʾ. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records this at both occurrences. Ibn al-Jazarī counts the two innī arānī expressions among the sūra's yāʾs before open hamza and records their opening among the Yūsuf forms.
12:36/q20 What does 'press' mean here? [أَعْصِرُ · meaning]
  12:36/q20/p1 It means squeezing something moist to extract its liquid. — reasons: Al-Layth distinguishes ʿaṣartu, doing it oneself, from iʿtaṣartu, having another do it; ʿuṣāra is extracted liquid. Al-Jishumi compares rain-bearing muʿṣirāt; Ibn ʿAshur explains ʿaṣīr as the product. Al-Biqaʿi likewise defines extraction. Ibn ʿAzīz glosses aʿṣiru as extract. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces ʿaṣr forms to pressure and extraction, comparing the vine, harvest year, rain clouds, whirlwind, and al-ʿAṣr.
12:36/q21 What does 'wine' mean as the thing pressed, and how is the wording explained? [أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا · meaning] (turns on: Whether khamr directly names grapes, anticipates wine, abbreviates a construction, or names the intended product.)
  12:36/q21/p1 It means grapes in a dialect, especially Oman or Azd Oman. — reasons: Al-Asmaʿi's Bedouin called carried grapes khamr; al-Dahhak says the Quran uses several peoples' speech. Some name Ghassan and Azd Oman, while Ibn al-Qasim says Quraysh knew it. This explains the object directly. Al-Zarkashī relays Ibn Durayd through al-Fārisī on the Azd Oman lexical usage and a view denying metaphor on that basis; al-Suyūṭī reports al-Ḍaḥḥāk's Omani gloss.
  12:36/q21/p2 Grapes are called wine by anticipating what they will become. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj compares naming a thing by its eventual product; al-Wahidi cites cooking bricks from clay and molasses or juice. Ibn al-Anbari and many commentators take this as the common explanation. Al-Sijistani's separate evidence notes masculine khamr among eloquent speakers. Ibn Jinnī treats wine as the grapes' effect, named in place of its cause; al-Zarkashī describes the grapes by their future wine, and al-Suyūṭī compares other things named by their future state.
  12:36/q21/p3 An omitted noun is understood: grapes intended for wine. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj and later authors supply the missing grapes; al-Qurtubi calls it an omitted genitive relation and adds khamra/khamr/khumur inflection.
  12:36/q21/p4 Wine itself may be called pressed because grapes are pressed for its sake. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba compares saying 'I pressed oil' for olives; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan permit the goal of pressing as its object. Al-Alusi says this differs from the common future-product explanation. Al-Zarkashī reports Ibn ʿAzīz's proposal that the transferred usage lies in the verb aʿṣiru, meaning to extract.
12:36/q22 What reading says 'grapes' in place of 'wine,' and what status does it have? [خَمْرًۭا · readings] (turns on: Whether the reported substitution is recited text or explanatory wording.)
  12:36/q22/p1 Ibn Masud and Ubayy are reported to read 'I press grapes.' — reasons: Al-Tabari and others cite Ibn Masud; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan add Ubayy. Al-Durr says Ibn Masud swore the Prophet gave him this wording. The reading makes grapes explicit. The Muḥtasab preface specifically notes Ibn Jinnī's defense of Ibn ʿAbbās's ʿinaban wording.
  12:36/q22/p2 The 'grapes' wording is an explanatory gloss, not a canonical recitation. — reasons: Abu Hayyan argues the mutawatir reading for both is khamr and ʿinab conflicts with the codex; al-Samin says the gloss does not establish synonymy, comparing the explanatory tharīd. Al-Alusi agrees.
12:36/q23 What did the baker see above his head? [أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِى خُبْزًۭا تَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ · reports] (turns on: Whether the report specifies three baskets, general bread, or tharīd.)
  12:36/q23/p1 Three baskets of bread or assorted food were above him, and birds ate from the upper one. — reasons: Muqatil mentions a top dish; others mention predatory birds. Reports vary between bread, mixed food and the exact basket arrangement; the upper basket is the one eaten. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid give the same overall scene.
  12:36/q23/p2 The scene is bread carried over his head and pecked or torn by birds. — reasons: Al-Baydawi and al-Tabataba'i keep the verse's simple detail; al-Razi says the scene matches the baker's trade. Al-Wajiz specifies birds of prey. Al-Dāmaghānī cites the bread above the head as an instance of literal carrying.
  12:36/q23/p3 The food may specifically have been tharīd. — reasons: Ibn ʿAtiyya cites Ibn Masud's codex; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi treat its wording as an explanatory gloss, not a canonical reading.
  12:36/q23/p4 The mention of bread anticipates the grain that birds actually eat. — reasons: Al-Zarkashī says the dreamer names bread although birds eat grain, by naming it for what the grain will become.
12:36/q24 What does 'above' mean in the baker's dream? [فَوْقَ · meaning]
  12:36/q24/p1 It means on or at the top. — reasons: Muqatil cites 8:12 and 14:26 for uppermost sense; Bursevi cites 8:12's 'above the necks.' Al-Dāmaghānī explicitly gives physical elevation above the head as a sense of fawq.
12:36/q25 How is the baker's bread clause constructed? [أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِى خُبْزًۭا تَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ · grammar]
  12:36/q25/p1 'Birds eat from it' describes the bread; 'above' may attach to carrying or stand circumstantially with bread. — reasons: Al-Samin gives both attachments for fawq.
12:36/q26 What does 'bread' denote here? [خُبْزًۭا · meaning]
  12:36/q26/p1 Prepared baked flour and water, a loaf. — reasons: Ibn ʿAshur defines the food; al-Biqaʿi calls it prepared food.
12:36/q27 How does Arabic use 'birds' here? [ٱلطَّيْرُ · grammar] (turns on: Whether ṭayr is exclusively collective or can also be singular.)
  12:36/q27/p1 Ṭayr is a feminine collective whose singular is ṭāʾir. — reasons: Al-Layth gives this acc

ount; Ahmad ibn Yahya and Abu Ubayda agree ṭāʾir means one bird.
  12:36/q27/p2 Ṭayr can itself be singular, with plural ṭuyūr. — reasons: Abu Ubayda uniquely permits this, as reported by al-Wahidi.
12:36/q28 How is the hamza in 'my head' read? [رَأْسِى · readings] (turns on: Retention or elision of hamza.)
  12:36/q28/p1 The standard reading retains the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER records it.
  12:36/q28/p2 Another canonical reading elides the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER notes classical Arabic allows this.
12:36/q29 How is the hamza in 'tell us' read? [نَبِّئْنَا · readings] (turns on: How the hamza is articulated.)
  12:36/q29/p1 The standard reading retains the hamza. — reasons: Al-Nahhas says hamzated nabbiʾnā retains yāʾ unless hamza is lightened or replaced; Qiraat-ER records standard hamza. Ibn al-Jazarī details Abu Jaʿfar's disputed routes for tahqīq of nabbiʾnā; Abū Ṭāhir, al-Hudhalī, Abū al-ʿIzz, Abū al-ʿAlā, and Ibn Mihrān transmit or discuss retention. Al-Aṣbahānī's Warsh route excepts nabbiʾ forms from substitution.
  12:36/q29/p2 A ten-reader canonical variant elides the hamza. — reasons: Qiraat-ER says the meaning remains; al-Nahhas discusses lightening and replacement. Ibn al-Jazarī explains Abū Jaʿfar's replacement of silent hamza with a preceding-vowel-matched long vowel and records substitution of nabbiʾnā through some routes.
12:36/q30 Why is 'tell us' plural when each had his own dream? [نَبِّئْنَا · rhetoric]
  12:36/q30/p1 The plural narrates their separate requests collectively. — reasons: Bursevi and al-Alusi compare messengers separately addressed in 23:51; al-Tabataba'i says repeated 'said' replaces a repeated request.
12:36/q31 What does 'its interpretation' mean? [بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · meaning]
  12:36/q31/p1 It is the dream's interpretation: the outcome or end to which what was seen leads. — reasons: Al-Tabari and Abu Ubayd derive taʾwīl from return; Ibn Abbas glosses interpretation. Al-Razi and al-Biqaʿi stress the eventual result, while Mujahid speaks of expression of the dream. Al-Dāmaghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī give dream interpretation as a sense of taʾwīl; Ibn al-Jawzī also cites the dream's later fulfillment in 12:100.
12:36/q32 What does the pronoun in 'its interpretation' refer to? [بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the singular pronoun summarizes both accounts or distributes over each dream.)
  12:36/q32/p1 It refers to the whole account or both visions, like a demonstrative 'that.' — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the singular pronoun collectively; Ibn ʿAshur allows the mentioned matter or dream as a class. Al-Alusi takes what was seen.
  12:36/q32/p2 Each man means his own dream. — reasons: Al-Samin reports this alternative; al-Tabataba'i says the pronoun contextually refers to what each saw.
12:36/q33 What did the prisoners mean by calling Joseph one of the beneficent? [إِنَّا نَرَىٰكَ مِنَ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether they praise observed conduct, intellectual skill, or the favor they hope he will perform.)
  12:36/q33/p1 He was kind to fellow prisoners and visibly virtuous. — reasons: Al-Tabari prefers this practical-kindness sense, explaining that interpretation would be a further favor; al-Dahhak, Qatada and many others mention treating sick people, consoling grief, making room, gathering aid, worship, and good speech. Al-Tabataba'i says signs of a pure heart made them trust his judgment; Islahi defines muhsin as one who acts before God.
  12:36/q33/p2 He was learned or skilled at interpreting dreams. — reasons: Al-Farra says learned; Ibn al-Anbari supplies 'in knowledge' and recalls his teaching; al-Zajjaj says skilled in interpretation. Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan call this the majority view. Ibn ʿAshur defines ihsan as proficiency and says they inferred ability from intelligence without proof. Asad calls it figurative usage.
  12:36/q33/p3 The praise is a polite, conditional appeal: interpret our dreams and thereby do us good. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and al-Farra read the praise prospectively; al-Tabari answers that the requested interpretation is kindness like Joseph's other acts. Qushayri says it seeks his beneficence.
12:36/q34 What specific acts made Joseph known as beneficent in prison? [ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ · reports]
  12:36/q34/p1 He cared for sick and distressed inmates, aided the needy, made space, urged patience and worshipped God. — reasons: Al-Dahhak adds practical aid and intercession; Qatada adds hope of reward, cleansing and devotion; al-Mawardi lists accepting excuses and putting others first; Ibn Kathir adds honesty and trustworthiness. Al-Tabataba'i reports borrowing for needy people and helping the weak. Al-Biqaʿi says inmates felt blessed by his company.
12:36/q35 Why did Joseph postpone interpreting the dreams? [نَبِّئْنَا بِتَأْوِيلِهِۦٓ · interpretation]
  12:36/q35/p1 He knew one interpretation would mean suffering and first diverted to a prophetic sign and monotheism. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabi, Baghawi and al-Wajiz connect the delay to the baker's fate. Al-Biqaʿi says Joseph used their receptiveness to counsel worship of God and rejection of partners first; al-Tabrisi invokes calling with wisdom (16:125).
12:36/q36 What lesson does Joseph's response give about teaching? [* · interpretation]

[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | كعبد الله means “in a state like ʿAbd Allāh”; poets may use ك as مثل under poetic necessity.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The ability to take مِن or على, as in بمن سواءك, supports treating these expressions as locative-like; ordinary adjectives do not fit the same pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أقبل قبلك means the caravan approaches your direction, while نحى نحوك means it is directed toward your side.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl accepts accusative قريب when it is treated as a locative, meaning a place near you.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports Arabs saying هل قريبا منك أحد, parallel to هل قربك أحد.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | دونك is not raised in its ordinary locative use; the source treats it as an extended comparison or substitution expression.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The original sense of locatives is an earthly place or settled location, extended in expressions like لصلب القناة and لمن شجرة صالحة.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Locative expressions include خلفك, قدامك, أمامك, تحتك, قبالتك, and ناحية الدار.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قصد قصدك behaves like نحى نحوك and أقبل قبلك and can be nominative or accusative; دون alone can also mean inferior.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Bare جوف, داخل, and خارج do not function as adverbs; they require في or من, unlike خلف and similar terms.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | خلف and related terms denote sides around a noun, so they can become adverbs or nouns; جوف and داخل instead resemble body-part terms.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | وسط الدار can be an adverb, but وسطه is a noun as shown by its direct-object use; في وسط الدار is a prepositional nominal phrase.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قبل, قصد, and ناحية more readily function as nouns than خلف, أمام, and تحت, though the latter usage is attested.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Rare locative terms include صددك for direction, سقبك for nearness, وزن الجبل for a side, and زنة الجبل for opposite.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قرابتك في العلم means “close to you in knowledge”; حذاءه and إزاءه mean facing him, while حوالية and أقطار describe surrounding regions.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī’s مساليه means the two

[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | شرقي حوران and اليمينا are locative accusatives meaning east of and on the right side; Sībawayh cites Jarīr and ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus transmits from Abū ʿAmr the interpretation of مجراها اليمينا as “on the right side,” and says it is Abū ʿAmr’s own view.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قصدك means “in your direction”; a line about the Pleiades and a report from reliable Arabs support this sense.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | جنابتا الأنف means the two lines flanking a gazelle’s nose; al-Aʿshā’s phrase جنبى فطيمة is parallel evidence for the two sides.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Locatives are accusative in the same structural way as measure expressions such as عشرين درهما and a quality complement such as عملا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The locative is governed by the place or predicate associated with it, paralleling the relation between subject and predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:وذاكلأنهاظروففيهاالأشياءوتكونفيهافانتصبلأنهPageV01P403#194/f9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | مكان فلان can mean “in his place,” namely a substitute who replaces him and performs his role.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a verb before its delayed dual subject, Arabic can leave the verb singular; this parallels Yusuf's singular وَدَخَلَ before فَتَيَانِ.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some Arabs add plural or dual pronouns to a verb even before a following plural subject, analogizing these markers to feminine tā; Sībawayh calls this usage rare.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الفرزدق | reports | Al-Farazdaq's verse, with يعصرن before أقاربه, attests to the rare plural verb marker before a following subject.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil extends the same agreement pattern to adjectives such as شاب, شيخ, and كهل when they mean duals or plurals.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | prefers | For dual or plural adjectives such as قرشي and كهل, al-Khalil prefers treating the form as a noun: قرشيان أبواه and كهلون أصحابه.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Those who use أكلوني البراغيث agreement extend it to adjectives, saying حسنين أبواه and قرشيين آباؤهم.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same competing adjective patterns apply to أفعَل forms such as أعور and أحمر, with dual forms such as أحمران before a following subject.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the noun precedes its predicate, the predicate shows full number agreement; the postposed pattern instead resembles a preceding verb with its following subject.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A form such as أعور آباؤه can be understood as if it were أعورين, although that form is not actually spoken; poetry attests to the construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | For this agreement, أعور قومك and صم قومه are better; broken plural adjectives like حسان act as nouns, not as verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Broken plurals such as حسان change the singular's form and behave like a single noun with collective meaning; regular -ون plurals better follow the preceding-verb pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | Where a plural is formed with wāw and nūn and leaves the singular stem intact, Sībawayh prefers the pattern of a preceding verb: منطلق قومه.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو ذؤيب الهذلي والفرزدق وأبو زبيد الطائي وبنو أسد والكميت بن معروف | reports | Poetic evidence for a singular masculine predicate before a plural noun includes Abu Dhuʾayb's مضطمرا, al-Farazdaq's طويلا, Abu Zubayd's مستحن, a poet of Asad's مسقى, and al-Kumayt's محمولا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Aʿsha, ʿAmir ibn Juwayn, and Tufayl al-Ghanawi offer poetic examples where feminine nouns lack feminine agreement marking; Sībawayh explains the omission by reliance on the noun itself.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A feminine predicate placed before its noun follows the same pattern as a masculine one, with feminine tā added.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f31] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil explains ما أحسن وجوههما by treating a dual as a plural, like two people saying نحن فعلنا ذاك; the form also distinguishes independent things from parts of one thing.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f33] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رؤبة | reports | Yunus reports that Ruʾbah said ما أحسن رأسيهما, another dual expression treated with plural agreement.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f34] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | وضعا رحالهما means the two mounts' saddlebags; speakers treat the two sets of gear as two things, though the unmarked phrasing would use singular رحلي.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dual and plural suffixes on predicates can correspond to verbal agreement markers, as alif and wāw do in قالا and قالوا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a following feminine subject, a verb takes feminine tā but no dual or plural suffix; with the noun first, the verb carries dual or plural pronouns.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Feminine tā is a gender marker, not a pronoun like dual alif or plural wāw, which explains why its presence and omission behave differently.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some Arabs omit feminine tā in long constructions, where mentioning the feminine noun itself makes the marking unnecessary.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Omission of feminine marking is rarer with singular living beings and more common with inanimates; the explicit feminine noun can suffice just as an explicit dual or plural noun does.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكمررتبرجلحسنأبواهوأحسنأبواهوأخارجقومك|فصارهذا#221/f9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Human collectives allow the pronouns هم and هن, while camels take هي or هن and feminine predicates rather than a human plural masculine pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says the vocative is already definite, which prevents the definite article from entering it.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The article in names such as النجم and الدبران remains separable, unlike the article integrated into the name الله.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil analyzes اللهم as a vocative in which م replaces يا; the ending behaves like a vocative particle embedded in the word.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In اللهم فاطر السماوات والأرض, the construction is understood on يا; frequent use has allowed this name several special forms. | mentions 39:46
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The added ألف and هاء in يا أيها reinforce the vocative particle as though يا were repeated around the noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الشاعر | reports | The poetic address يا التي is compared with يا الله, illustrating the exceptional vocative form.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as يا خباث and يا لكاع are definite vocative names corresponding to feminine descriptions such as يا فاسقة and يا خبيثة.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some expressions belong only to vocative use, including يا نومان and يا هناه; their restriction to address supports their status as definite names.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus heard Arabs say يا فاسق الخبيث, which Sibawayh treats as further evidence that يا فاسق is definite.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A definite vocative lacks tanwin; tanwin disting

[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A bare vocative such as يا رجل or يا فاسق means the same as يا أيها الرجل or يا أيها الفاسق and is definite by direct address.

[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ذو الرمة | reports | Dhu al-Rumma's أدارا is evidence for tanwin on an indefinite vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · توبة بن الحمير | reports | Tawba ibn al-Humayyir's يا تيسا is another poetic example of an indefinite vocative with tanwin.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Abd Yaghuth's يا راكبا illustrates tanwin on an indefinite vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | In يا دار أقوت, al-Tirimmah treats what follows as a new statement about the addressed house, not as its adjective, explaining the absent tanwin.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأحوص | reports | Al-Ahwas's يا دار حسرها also addresses the house and then makes a separate statement rather than describing it adjectivally.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عمرو بن قنعاس | reports | In يا بيت بالعلياء بيت, the locative phrase is not an adjective; the poet means that he has a house in al-Aliyāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f27] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأحوص | reports | Al-Ahwas's tanwin on يا مطر is poetic; the name remains nominative, like a declinable noun in a nominative position, rather than becoming an indefinite accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f28] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عيسى بن عمر | reports | Isa ibn Umar analyzes يا مطرا like يا رجلا as an indefinite vocative; Sibawayh says the analogy is possible but reports no Arab attestation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An annexed vocative such as يا عشرين رجلا follows the pattern of يا ضاربا رجلا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With coordinated vocative names, a following dual adjective may be accusative or nominative, as in يا زيد وعمرو الطويلين.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a demonstrative and a coordinated name, الطوال is raised by coordination; it is not the same construction as an adjective after يا هؤلاء.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An adjective behaves like the definite article by identifying its noun, while coordination does not; the adjective can be understood as a relative clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A proper name following its noun is not equivalent to an adjective with the definite article because the name is independently definite.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil distinguishes يا أيها الرجل وزيد الرجلين الصالحين by their different grammatical positions; if they matched, the second construction would use ذو الجمة.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A noun with the definite article is normally barred from direct address, with الله as the exception because its article is inseparable and frequent.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكياأيهاالرجلوعبداللهالمسلمينالصالحين|وهذابمنزلة#293/f9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh proposes إله as the underlying name of Allah, with the initial alif deleted and the article taking its place.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن and its sisters resemble verbs in how they govern following words, but they are not verbs and do not conjugate like verbs; the comparison is to nouns that resemble verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An initial إن اليوم زيدا منطلق cancels اليوم, as in an initial nominal sentence; when اليوم is governed by إن, it can precede a separate subject and predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن اليوم فيه زيد ذاهب keeps اليوم under إن's governance, as shown by the accusative in إن عمرا فيه زيد متكلم and the nominative opening اليوم فيه زيد.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The predicate locative phrase لفيها can be canceled, allowing إن زيدا لفيها قائما to mean إن زيدا لقائم فيها.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abu Zubayd's verse puts the emphatic lām into a phrase that can only be canceled, confirming that لفيها may likewise be canceled.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With إن زيدا فيها لقائم, nominative is required because the lām makes the sentence depend on إن; accusative would wrongly license فيها زيد لقائما as an opening sentence.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil explains إن بك زيد مأخوذ as an ellipsis for إنه بك زيد مأخوذ, comparable to poetic constructions that require a pronoun to be understood.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ابن صريم اليشكري | reports | Ibn Suraym al-Yashkuri's verse كأن ظبية illustrates the poetic ellipsis compared with إن بك زيد مأخوذ.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | A second poem has كأن ثدياه حقان; Sībawayh says the construction is only acceptable with an understood pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil compares this ellipsis with al-Farazdaq's ولكن زنجى; accusative زنجيا is more common, understood as لا يعرف قرابتي.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says إن and its sisters govern both accusative and nominative, as كان does, but unlike كان they cannot take an implicit nominative or place the predicate first in the same way.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | Accusative طالبا is better than nominative زنجى in this ellipsis: if a phrase were suppressed, it would be made light and the suppressed expression would be predicative.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿsha's أن هالك deletes an object pronoun; Sībawayh says the deletion marks omitted pronominal reference rather than turning أن into an introductory particle.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · رؤبة ابن العجاج | reports | With ليتما زيدا منطلق, cancellation is acceptable; Ruʾbah recited the poem with رفع هذا, either like مثلا ما بعوضة or إنما زيد منطلق.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | لعلما acts like كأنما; Ibn Kuraʿ's verse supplies an attestation of this form.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says إنما does not govern what follows, just as أرى when used without its ordinary force does not govern; the construction treats the particle and ما as a unit.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · المرار الفقعسي | reports | Al-Murar al-Faqʿasi's بعدما shows ما joining with the preceding word as one particle, after which the next phrase begins independently.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When إن is lightened, it behaves like لكن and takes lām to distinguish it from negative إن.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f29] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · من نثق به | reports | A trusted transmitter reports hearing Arabs say إن عمرا لمنطلق.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The construction كأن أخوك عبد الله is unavailable because these particles do not inflect or contain an implicit nominative as كان does; they are only verb-like in their effect on what follows.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When إن زيدا is followed by an adjective but no overt predicate, the adjective becomes the predicate; its accusative parallels the adjective after كان w

hen its predicate is omitted.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With إن فيها زيدا قائما, the locative phrase may be treated as canceled, allowing قائما or قائم; alternatively the subject may be delayed after إن زيدا فيها.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The explanation of nominative versus accusative here follows the rules of the opening nominal sentence; فيها can make the utterance complete but is not itself the subject as هذا is.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An expression can occupy another expression's syntactic position without sharing its case: يقول ذاك occupies the place of قائل after رجل.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In إن بك زيدا مأخوذ and إن لك زيدا واقف, بك and لك are not stable locations or positions for Zayd when the intended meaning is being taken or standing.
[SIBAWAYH:وهيمنالفعلms242بمنزلةعشرينمنالأسماءالتيبمنزلةالفعللاتصرفتصرف#268/f9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The phrase إن فيك زيدا لراغب follows the same analysis: the locative phrase is canceled as in the opening sentence, with the omitted construction understood as إن زيدا راغب.

[ITQAN:v4p333/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | People derived dream interpretation from Joseph’s dreams and prison companions’ visions; when the Quran did not resolve a case, they used explanatory Sunnah, sayings and proverbs, considering customary usage indicated by the command to observe recognized practice.
